decisions.question: How many tasks, split where? The cap is 6 (Global Constraint 3), every task but the last must start with a failing test, and the Scope asks for property tests (cycles against brute-force reachability, G17's removal property, order independence).

options.label: Five tasks, property tests inside
options.consequence: One task per analysis family, leaves first (cycles; self-references; writer conflicts with scope violations, which share one owner list; analyzeTopologyGraph with findTopicNameCollisions), then the gate and verification doc. Each property test joins the task whose analysis it checks and fails there first because the stub throws.

options.label: Six tasks, a separate property-test task
options.consequence: The property-test task could not start with a failing test, because the analyses would already pass it (Global Constraint 1).

options.label: Six tasks, conflicts and violations apart
options.consequence: Two tasks build the same owner list; a reviewer could not reject one while approving the other in any useful way.

decisions.why: Matches the seams S142 suggested and the right-sizing rule (split only where a reviewer could reject one task and approve its neighbour); keeps Global Constraint 1 true for every property test.
evidence: docs/auto-run/steps/S142.json notes_for_orchestrator (FOR THE PLAN WRITER, item 6)

decisions.question: Which strongly-connected-components algorithm, and recursive or not?

options.label: Iterative Tarjan
options.consequence: Linear; the depth-first path lives in two lists, so any chain length works (a ring of 300000 in 0.7 s); about 50 lines with a non-obvious loop, so the plan gives its body.

options.label: Recursive Tarjan
options.consequence: Shorter, but overflows the stack at a ring of 10000 topologies under dart test (F1) while passing every conformance case.

options.label: Warshall reachability closure
options.consequence: Simplest to read, cubic in topologies; it is the property test's oracle, so the test would compare an algorithm with itself.

decisions.why: The governance names strongly connected sets and asks for a brute-force reachability check as the property oracle; a long catalog chain must not crash activation or the workspace scan. Settled by experiment: the first draft was recursive and failed at 10000.

decisions.question: Which topics does a cycle list? The Interface says 'the topics one member writes and another reads'.

options.label: Written by one member, read by a different member
options.consequence: A member's own self-read is not listed unless another member reads it; a topic between a member and an outsider is not listed; topics collected in a set, so each once (routed item from S135).

options.label: Written by a member and read by any member
options.consequence: A member's self-read joins the cycle's topics, mixing the inter-topology finding with the intra-topology one the Interface keeps apart.

decisions.chosen: Written by one member, read by a different member
decisions.why: 'another' contrasts with 'one member', and arcs exist only between distinct topologies (Analyses, Cycles). The conformance case has no member self-read, so the reading is pinned by Task 1's own test; the dry run's D2 passes the gate's replay.

decisions.question: How do the cycles come out in 'the order of the first of its ids'?

options.label: Sort after the search
options.consequence: Sort the cycles by compareTopologyIds of their first (smallest) id; total, since components are disjoint. Task 1's first test builds a graph where Tarjan completes the later-named cycle first.

options.label: Rely on the search order
options.consequence: Tarjan completes components in reverse topological order; the conformance case happens to agree, so the dry run's D1 passes the gate's replay but returns the wrong order on other graphs.

decisions.why: The order is the contract's, not an accident of the visit order.

decisions.question: How does findSelfReferences find 'every edge on any unmediated path', and how does a read match its topic?

options.label: Forward and backward passes
options.consequence: Edges are in dependency order (G6), so one forward pass (reached from a read through edges bearing no state) and one backward pass (reaching a write through such edges) mark them; an edge is on a path exactly when both do. Linear. A read matches by TopicInput.topic, whatever its dedup; a write is an edge bearing no state whose output is the topic.

options.label: Enumerate every path
options.consequence: Direct but exponential in the worst case; it is the property test's oracle instead.

options.label: Forward pass only
options.consequence: Lists edges that lead to another topic's write (the dry run's D3 fails one G14 case and passes the other and the G17 sample).

decisions.why: Exact by construction, linear, and checked against a walk of every path over 500 seeds; matching by topic keeps a dedup read a read of its topic (dry run D4 shows the suite would miss it).

decisions.question: How are writer conflicts and scope violations computed?

options.label: One owner list per state topic
options.consequence: _owners(graph, topic): topologies writing it (TopologySource with their scope) in graph order, then claims claiming it, one entry per claim; empty for event and replay topics. Conflicts are topics of graph.topics with two or more owners; violations iterate owners and readers.

options.label: Two separate scans
options.consequence: The same owner rules written twice, free to drift apart.

decisions.chosen: One owner list per state topic
decisions.why: Spec §3.11 and §7.2 define one notion of owner for both checks (Refinement 3); graph.claims already keeps equal claims, so 'one entry per claim' falls out (routed item from S141).

decisions.question: Scope violations are 'Ordered by topic, then owner, then reader'. How do two owners with one source and two scopes order (one service claiming unbound and bound to a module), and how are equal owners counted?

options.label: Source rendering, then scope; equal owners once
options.consequence: Matches the claim order's tie-break after the source; a Set literal drops the equal violations of equal owners in iteration order (the G16 case's two page:form claims give one violation per reader). Reported as a low contract gap: the tie-break is not in the text.

options.label: Source rendering, then graph order of the owners
options.consequence: Topologies before claims for one source cannot happen (distinct prefixes), so this equals the first for claims (claim order is source then scope) but states nothing; same gap.

options.label: Stop and ask
options.consequence: Blocks the plan on a tie the conformance suite never builds.

decisions.chosen: Source rendering, then scope; equal owners once
decisions.why: The only reading consistent with the canonical claim order; pinned by Task 3's test. An analysis's result order is in topology-ir@v1's Breaking list, so the text should name the tie-break; compatible to add (no fixture builds the tie). The signal that would change my mind: the owner wanting violations grouped by claim rather than by owner.

decisions.question: How does findTopicNameCollisions order names, count repeats and read its argument?

options.label: String.compareTo names, a map of sets, one pass
options.consequence: Names in code-unit order (the order the canonical topic order uses for names); a TopicDeclaration is a value, so a repeat is one element; a lazy iterable from a scanner is read once.

options.label: Names in first-seen order
options.consequence: Not 'ordered by name'; the dry run's D11 passes the gate's replay.

decisions.chosen: String.compareTo names, a map of sets, one pass
decisions.why: Interface: 'ordered by name'; G18: 'counts a repeated declaration once'; nidana.model.11 read graph arguments once for the same reason.

decisions.question: Which results are unmodifiable?

options.label: Every analysis, empty included
options.consequence: List.unmodifiable everywhere; one G3 test per analysis (routed item from S141).

options.label: analyzeTopologyGraph only
options.consequence: Passes G3's case, which only clears analyzeTopologyGraph's result; the dry run's D8 shows a growable findScopeViolations passes the gate's replay.

decisions.why: G3 covers findings and the Analyses section says 'every returned list is unmodifiable'.

decisions.question: How are the property tests built: generator, oracles, seed count, floors, and how does G17's removal property get clean graphs?

options.label: One seeded generator, independent oracles, greedy clean graphs, floors near half of F2
options.consequence: test/src/analysis_support.dart with dart:math Random(seed), 500 seeds (as lineage_property_test.dart); Warshall closure for cycles, a walk of every path for self-references; G17 over graphs grown topology by topology and claim by claim while they stay clean; floors at about half of what the seeds reach, so the properties cannot turn vacuous silently.

options.label: G17 over whichever generated graphs happen to be clean
options.consequence: Most generated graphs have a finding; the property would rest on few, mostly tiny, graphs.

options.label: No floors
options.consequence: A generator change could make a property pass vacuously.

decisions.chosen: One seeded generator, independent oracles, greedy clean graphs, floors near half of F2
decisions.why: No new dependency (ADR-002 item 3; package:test has no generator); the oracles differ from the implementations; F2 measured the counts (225 graphs with a cycle, 180 unmediated and 701 mediated self-reads, 90 grown clean graphs of three parts or more).

decisions.question: The Interface gives dartdoc only to analyzeTopologyGraph. What do the other five public functions carry?

options.label: A // comment naming the rule and guarantee
options.consequence: The public documentation stays exactly the Interface's; the comment follows the == comments of nidana.model.10 and .11.

options.label: New dartdoc
options.consequence: Public docs that the contract does not state.

decisions.chosen: A // comment naming the rule and guarantee
decisions.why: Run rules: dartdoc carried from a contract's Interface is copied as written; nothing says to add public documentation beyond it.

decisions.question: How much code does the plan carry? Precedent plans (nidana.model.11) wrote every body; the writing-plans skill asks for signatures, exact test code and a body only for an algorithm the signature and tests do not determine.

options.label: Exact tests, one algorithm body, the rest by signature and approach
options.consequence: The test files are the drafts the dry run ran, filled by fill_plan.py so they cannot drift; _components (the iterative search) is given whole; every other helper by signature, the expression that matters, and its decision. 1722 lines against a 1555-line derivative.

options.label: Every body, as nidana.model.11's plan did
options.consequence: About 280 more lines of library code the implementer would only copy; the skill calls that a transcript.

decisions.chosen: Exact tests, one algorithm body, the rest by signature and approach
decisions.why: Opus implementers on a full-review tier; the generator must be exact because the floors depend on every Random call; the iterative loop is the one place a reasonable implementer could get it subtly wrong.

decisions.question: Does this phase pin G22's clause that the analyses create no timer and schedule no microtask?

options.label: No new test
options.consequence: D6's purity_test.dart already rejects every scheduling token under lib/, the analyses are synchronous, and G22's case first replays at nidana.model.14 (unrestricted).

options.label: A zone-counting test now
options.consequence: One more test for a guarantee another phase's gate replays.

decisions.why: Nothing the analyses do can schedule, and two checks already exist; the verification doc says so under Outstanding.

contract_gaps.where: hsdd/contract/topology-ir.md line 436 (Analyses, Scope violations: 'Ordered by topic, then owner, then reader'), with G16 and the Versioning Breaking list (line 470: 'an analysis's semantics or result order')
contract_gaps.problem: An owner is a source with a scope, and two owners can share a source (one service claiming unbound and bound to a module). The canonical order of message sources ties them, so the result order of findScopeViolations is not fixed by the text for that input; two conforming implementations can differ. No fixture builds the tie. Low: no consumer depends on the order within such a tie today.
contract_gaps.proposed_fix: hsdd-contract, compatible within v1: 'Ordered by topic, then owner by its source's rendering and then its scope (application, module, page), then reader', optionally with one G16 case building the tie. nidana.model.12 implements this reading (plan decision 8).
